Regarding the Absence of a Good Manuscript for the Cundī Repentance Rite: Why is it that there has been no good manuscript? The World-Honored One said:
"This is the Great Yoga Teaching of the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana, the Samaya Consecration Mandala, and the Secret Dharma Gate of the Tathāgata. It is thus accomplished.
This is the essential core of the Buddha’s mind. Yet, worldly teachers, measuring it with shallow intellect, merely accommodate those of initial capacity;
they do not realize that it directly addresses those of superior faculties who transcend the mundane and enter the sacred. Thus, one realizes the difficulty of embodying its fundamental purport.

Although the fundamental, subtle wheel of syllables employs written characters, these are all words whose meaning transcends all signs; their self-nature is empty space, and they are likewise not [limited by] form.
To give rise to a mind that is like space is the essential point of the World-Honored One’s separate transmission outside the teachings.

Yet, when worldly masters seek it through written words, they transform contemplation and practice into mere names and phrases, and invert the divine essence into mere sounds and rhythms; thus, the difficulty of transcending name and form arises.
Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, from within the Vidyādhara-piṭaka, briefly extracted the Great Mantras and the ritual procedures for their accomplishment. As for all precepts and practices...

The procedures for generating the bodhicitta, arranging the seed-syllables (*bīja*), forming mudrās, performing recitation and repentance (*sāmayika*), and entering the wisdom of *samādhi* each have their own established regulations.
Yet, the masters of the world cling to their traditions and treat the extant texts on specific repentances with general negligence; thus, it is difficult to faithfully observe the ritual protocols.
Aside from the sūtras and dhāraṇīs translated by Divākara, there are those translated by Vajrabodhi, Amoghavajra, Kumārajīva, Xuanzang, Tianxizai, Dharma-xian, and Vajradhvaja.
Their phrasing and citations differ; their recitations include annotations; their pronunciations contain long and short vowels;

and their characters vary in weight. When worldly masters produce sounds and rhythms at random, they frequently deviate from the Sanskrit phonology; thus, one must provide definitive character-by-character resolution.

The difficulty regarding sound is as follows: The scriptures explain the sequence of recitation, contemplative practice, and offerings, stating that one must first receive and uphold the prohibitive precepts, remaining firm and non-retrogressive with an undistracted mind, before being permitted to enter this Dharma gate.

Now, worldly practitioners bring their wives and children, drink alcohol and eat meat, failing to distinguish between the ordained and the laity, thereby defiling the ritual altars. Thus, the strict observance of the precepts is difficult.

Furthermore, the Elder Tianxi was rigorous in his observance of the precepts and had deeply penetrated the wisdom of contemplation. He exhausted the ultimate principles without being hindered by them; he realized emptiness without falling into nihilism.
If there were distinctions in a single meaning, he would examine the various scriptures exhaustively; if there were a discrepancy in a single character, he would investigate it for years.
He elucidated the Dharma through ten chapters and sustained himself with the three mysteries. Observing his sudden transcendence of the stages and his swift liberation from the fetters—
"Ke" refers to the profound mastery of spiritual transformations by Master Xingxiu.
That the Exoteric Teachings and Esoteric Sects encompass both essence and phenomena is the "Essential Heart of Universal Penetration" by Master Fazhuang.

That a single word explains the subtleties of a thousand gates and many words summarize the returns of the five sections is the "Perfect Cause" of the Vajradhvaja Secret Mantra. Formless Samādhi... [text truncated]
Like the full moon, the meaning of Buddha-nature is vast, empty, and luminous; this is the Perfect Teaching of the Exoteric and Esoteric (Xianmi Yuanzong) of the Venerable Nāgārjuna.
When this practice is compared to other schools, it is like Mount Sumeru towering over all other peaks, or a spiritual radiance eclipsing all other lights—how could these not be mere empty words?
Formerly, while serving under the teachings at Tianxi, I returned to recount my former learning in eighteen chapters.
He personally sought out the Elder for critique and correction, engaging in a dialogue that frequently reached several thousand words.

He thoroughly mastered the esoteric sections and deeply contemplated the intent of the contemplative teachings, cross-referencing them with the *Prajñāpāramitā-naya* and aligning them with the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the king of tantras.
Wherever the two men’s perspectives conflicted, they weighed them with impartiality; whatever required revision was revised, and whatever remained as it was...
The successor continues the succession. My years are advanced and my learning has become desolate; my friends have scattered like stars.
Among those who share my aspirations, there is none who observes me with such impartiality as Tianxi. If not for him, to whom else could I turn?
As Xingfashan Bencheng requested these few words from me to precede his [inscription], I have thus recounted the sincerity of my lifelong inclinations. As for the height of the tree—
"Seeking fame; the gate and courtyard are divided by partisan strife—this is not something known only to the two of us.
Written in the eighth month of autumn in the eighth year of the Kangxi era (Jiyou), by Xingchun and Fanxiang, as a preface to the *Xingfa of the Cundī Samādhi*.
Now, these dhāraṇī mantras emerge from the mouths of those who have attained the stage of fruition. Were it not for Padmanetra, one could not perceive their limits;
were it not for Vajrapāṇi, one could not grasp their essence. Yet, the verses and phrases differ in being either extensive or concise:

in the extensive version, a multitude of words does not constitute redundancy, while in the concise version, a single word does not constitute deficiency. How could this be anything other than what is called "the Great being identical to the Small"?

One does not perceive its boundaries; the smallest is identical to the great. For one who has forgotten and severed all objective realms, there is no benefit that cannot be obtained through sincere recitation and upholding.
This is like the Cundī-dhāraṇī: though the Sanskrit characters are few, its efficacy is most supreme.

The version translated by Vajrabodhi records this in detail. However, since dhāraṇīs belong to the category of *dhāraṇī*, they are termed "esoteric. One must know that as for totality, nothing is more total than this.

The true nature is most profound and secret within the doctrine of Mind-Only (*cittamātra*). If one perceives this mind and it merges back into the ground of nature (*prakṛti*), then there will be no sin to be extinguished and no merit to be produced.

How can those who receive and uphold [the teachings] fail to recognize the essential point of contemplating the mind, instead making the ritual altar, mudrās, dhāraṇīs, and vocal recitation their sole pursuit?
The Dharma Master Tianxi Jingchun, based on the three [texts] transmitted through the Tiantai and Tiantong lineages...
Master Mei composed the ritual manual for the recitation of Cundī. When about to enter the altar, one must first ensure that their ethical discipline (*śīla*) is pure.

Once having entered the altar, it is further necessary to clearly distinguish between the ordained and the laity. If the three virtues are assembled, they are inherently natural; if the ten vehicles are sealed, they are especially wondrously harmonized.
When the assembly present according to the occasion practices in accordance with the Dharma, they will attain inconceivable efficacy through a mind free from grasping and attachment.
It is as swift as a sound; it is truly sufficient for right faith and understanding. For when the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, he reveals the Truth through phenomena:
how could a square altar of four cubits not be the Dharmakāya? How could the reflection appearing in a mirror not be Prajñā? When burning incense and scattering flowers...
What is not liberation? The wise attain it through every touch; the ignorant look upon it and remain in self-delusion. Now, Master Jing takes up the contemplation of the mind to illuminate this:
one shall see that immeasurable Buddhas all flow forth from the vocal sounds of the practitioner’s own mind.

How much more so, then, regarding the fulfillment of all petitions within the gateway of worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)—what could possibly fail to be achieved? Only later did he come to know the Great Cundī.

It is like the King of Wish-Fulfilling Jewels (*cintāmaṇi-rāja*), which produces abundance and reaches everywhere without exception; it is the fruit proclaimed by seventy million Buddhas’ Mothers (*buddhamātṛkā*).
From every syllable, light is emitted in all directions, penetrating the void and piercing through metal and stone.

What is most precious is for a person to open the eye of the discernment of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya-cakṣus*) and skillfully bring it forth. Thus, the image of the moon’s orb already appears upon the master’s fingertip; as for the practitioner who walks this path—
Aspired to by me.

Compiled by the Bhikṣu Tianxi, Shou Deng. Section One:
Exhortation to Practice.
This Great Dhāraṇī has been spoken, is being spoken, and will be spoken by all Buddhas of the three periods of time; I, Śākyamuni, do likewise.
It is taught that this is for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings, so that they may attain entry into Bodhi.

Now, if all sentient beings who have not yet planted roots of goodness and lack the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) can recite and uphold [this teaching] even once or twice, the sprouts of their roots of goodness will emerge, and they will possess a share in Bodhi.
As for renunciant bodhisattvas, the supramundane siddhi sought in the present life—namely, the manifestation of concentration and wisdom—will be realized.
Regarding those who realize the stages (*bhūmi*) and *pāramitās*, and perfect unexcelled *bodhi*:

for a lay bodhisattva, what is sought in the present life is constant rebirth in the celestial realms, or becoming a king among men, drawing near to sages and worthies, being protected by the devas, having no calamities or misfortunes in the world, and having no sorrow or anxiety in the mind.
If one wishes to extinguish the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), the ten evil deeds, and all grave offenses, and to accumulate the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*):
Possessing the immeasurable merit of the six perfections, they are those for whom the great bodhisattvas preach the Dharma and who are constantly followed by the Buddhas of the ten directions.
If there are those who wish to cause kings, ministers, elders, householders, and others to give rise to a heart of love and respect [for the Buddha], [they should recite this].
Raising the intention for their benefit and happiness, may they all achieve fulfillment according to their aspirations.

For those whose stores of merit are incomplete, whose lifespans are short, who seek office but do not advance, and who are beset by manifold sufferings—may they obtain in this very life the blessings of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), possess the marks of longevity, attain high rank and position, and have all matters be auspicious.
May their supreme vows be such that water cannot drown them and fire cannot [consume them].
It can burn away poisons, weapons, enemies, and epidemics so that none of these cause harm; it can even transform evil into good.
To achieve this, one should, within a place of practice (*dōjō*), establish a formal commitment regarding specific matters and, with single-minded diligence, cultivate this Cundī Samādhi.
Indeed, this *dhāraṇī* is the secret treasury of all Buddhas of the three periods of time and the seven *koṭi* of Tathāgatas.
Because it provides a comprehensive exposition of the three bodies (trikāya), Nāgārjuna considered it to encompass the twenty-five schools in their entirety.
As for those who practice this specific school in particular, it is like a wish-fulfilling jewel; the most supreme among treasures, those who go to sea to gather gems must first seek this one.
Now that you have been able to hear this most supreme Dharma, you must certainly resolve to apply yourself with single-minded devotion, honoring and revering it so as to cultivate and realize it.
In a mere thought-moment, one may leave birth and death behind; within a single lifetime, one may decisively attain samādhi. Therefore, you should disregard even your own body and life.
One must strive with all one's might to take precedence; how could one instead remain negligent and indolent, waiting for another time?
The *Second Ritual for Recitation on Receiving Precepts and Arousing the Bodhicitta* states:
"Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who have previously maintained the practice of the precepts, if they enter the ritual arena, must further..."

One must vow and receive the precepts. If one is a layperson, upon first entering the *daochang* (meditation hall), one must likewise make vows according to one’s capacity and receive the Three Refuges and Five Precepts, or observe the Eightfold Fasting Precepts (*poṣadha*).

Therefore, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* (Fangdeng Sanmei) instructs that one should rely on a single master who is learned in both internal and external Vinaya to confess and receive the twenty-four precepts.
Thus, it is known that those wishing to enter the *daochang* must once again solemnly adorn themselves with the precepts.
The Dharma states: "If one's *śīla* (precepts) is not pure, *samādhi* will not manifest. This was the clear instruction of former Buddhas, and it is most fitting that you honor and uphold it.
Once you have received the precepts, you should give rise to the vast mind of *bodhicitta* and practice the conduct of a *bodhisattva*.
Now, as for this *bodhicitta*, it is the direct cause for attaining Buddhahood and the root of wisdom. Therefore, from this day forward until the attainment of perfect enlightenment...
Awakening consists solely in taking the Four Great Vows as one's essential resolve. With these great vows held in mind, the principles of reality become clear and penetrating.

As the *Bodhicitta Precepts Ritual* states: "All phenomena are without self and are equal like space; the mind is fundamentally unborn, its nature being perfect quiescence (*parinirvāṇa*) within emptiness.

One should know that the state where the nature is empty and perfectly quiescent is precisely the moment when the path of resonance and response intersects. When the path of resonance and response intersects, Bodhi—

This is the very tip of the mind’s focus. Therefore, one gives rise to kindness and extends compassion; seeking the Way above while transforming those below, one extensively cultivates the six perfections and dwells tranquilly in the single suchness.
By departing from the three obstacles, one attains purity; by manifesting the three virtues, one realizes their perfect fusion. From the beginning to the end, nothing exists outside of this.
These two dharmas—receiving the precepts and generating the bodhicitta—are the essential gateways for practitioners to initiate their practice. They stand as... [the standard].
This is the proper state for the mind; one should naturally restrain the mind and receive instruction, broadening the intellect and opening it to clarity.
If one remains muddled and superficial, failing to reflect and discern, this will not only render one's ascetic practices in vain, but will also greatly create various obstacles and difficulties.
Third, regarding the practitioner’s commitment to the ritual, the date, time, and duration:
once the practitioner of the mantra has obtained external protection and entrusted the administrative affairs [to others], they should select ten companions and return.

With one heart and unified resolve, they shall be as if riding a single boat. Furthermore, another ācārya should be specially invited to serve as an instructor (namely, a master of the *vaipulya-samādhi* who clarifies both the internal and external rules of discipline).
He shall demonstrate the path of clear contemplation and eliminate hindrances and obstacles. In the past, monastics and laypeople practiced together in the same place;
if there are now lay followers practicing together, one should establish boundary markers to separate them. Although they follow the same path, [they must remain distinct].
They shall not share the same ritual space or seating, for although laypeople may have received some portion of the precepts, they have not yet perfected the protocols of the Path;
their movements would be discordant and would instead cause disturbance. Do not compel them to comply by virtue of power or status, nor yield to them out of personal sentiment.

Even among the monastic community, those who are unworthy must be winnowed out; how much more so for the lay populace, where intermixture is easily tolerated? Lately, I have observed that customs have become lax and disordered, with many things failing to accord with the Dharma.
If one wishes for the sacred teachings to manifest clearly, one ought to be careful regarding the beginning from this point forward.

Regarding the dates: the sutras clarify periods of seven days, fourteen days, and even up to forty-nine days; however, the *Gongyuantongji* (Collection on Universal Penetration) establishes [the period] as one hundred and twenty days.
Ten days. Now, according to the Dharma, one must examine the capacity of the practitioner and determine a period of twenty-one days as the duration for a session of intensive cultivation.

One week, two weeks, increasing up to seven weeks, all depending on the individual's strength; however, these are merely the time limits for a beginner’s course. Those who practice throughout their entire lives need not necessarily follow this entirely.
Furthermore, prior to the formal cultivation, one must perform preparatory practices (*upāya*); if one does not strictly purify body and mind, [the practice will not succeed].
If one is well-versed in the ritual protocols but fails to enter the *maṇḍala* (place of practice), the path-mind will not be awakened and there will be no spiritual response or descent of grace.
Therefore, during the first seven days, one must first sever all worldly involvements, reduce sleep, moderate food intake, and subdue the mind.

Furthermore, one should recite and study the texts of repentance, investigate and explicate the path of contemplation, and continue to seek the protective empowerment of the Triple Gem, so that progress on the path may be free from demonic interference. In this way, one may hope for...
When samādhi and wisdom manifest before one, the siddhis are fully accomplished. Regarding the timing:
the Sūtra states that one should recite and maintain the practice according to the ritual rules three times, four times, or six times a day to seek mundane and supramundane siddhis.
Thus, three sessions by day and three by night constitute the universal rule for those engaged in cultivation.
The Fourth Section on the Emergence of the Correct Method of Practice.

This sūtra consists of one hundred thousand verses in its Sanskrit original. Although the current three Chinese translations are extremely concise and abbreviated, an examination of the three dharma-gates of performing rites (*kriyā*), grasping signs (*nimitta*), and non-arising (*anutpāda*) reveals that they are complete and without deficiency. Furthermore, regarding the efficacy of the ritual procedures and the grasping of...

The characteristics are somewhat more detailed; therefore, practitioners of mantra in the Western Land (India) extensively compiled the altar rituals, mudrās, and mantras of various sections, arranging them in sequence to supplement the root mantras as methods for contemplative practice.
This is called the *Japa-vidhi* (Ritual for Recitation), which was translated and transmitted to the Eastern Land (China).

In recent times, everyone has been accustomed to this practice; there have been instances of transformation through influence, yet for the most part, people remain mired in the dharma. Consequently, it is not without the fault of focusing exclusively on altar rituals and seals, or of being biased toward the sounds and characters of recitation.
This is truly because they have not yet grasped the principle that contemplation of reality (*li-guan*) is primary and that recitation and retention are secondary.

Regarding the present method: although the three types of repentance rituals must proceed in mutual dependence, the contemplation of the principle of non-arising (*anutpāda*) truly serves as the precursor.

That the nature of all phenomena is empty and that the myriad practices are without action is established as the standard for the perfect cause; it is taken as the ultimate destination for the great fruit.
Nevertheless, when comparing the present established method with the liturgical manuals recited in the past, the names and numbers do not differ, nor do the sequences.

These differ from one another; therefore, first cite the *Jingyi* (Ritual Manual for Recitation) to correspond with this [text], and then properly set forth the ten intentions for practicing the cultivation in successive order.
Within that *Jingyi*, the initial construction of the maṇḍala corresponds to the present method of purifying the ritual site (*do-chang*).

Next, entering the ritual site, one first pays homage to the Buddha, repents, rejoices in merit, entreats [the Buddhas to teach], makes vows, and dedicates the merit; this corresponds to the present "Paying Homage to the Buddha."

The sixth [section] is omitted. The fivefold repentance is moved to the eighth. Next, the arrangement of seats and the mudrās and mantras of the three divisions correspond to the current general prostration to the Triple Gem and the protection of the body;
this is the second [section], the purification of the three karmas. The boundary-binding corresponds to what is now included within the adornment of the ritual site.
The invitation corresponds to the current fourth [section], the invitation to the Triple Gem and the various devas. The five offerings correspond to the current third [section].
This is the offering of karma (*karma-pūjā*). This is the fifth, the praise in Sanskrit (*brahma-stotra*).
The recitation of arranged syllables and sounds is now the seventh, the mantra-recitation (*dhāraṇī-japa*). The recitation of *samādhi* has been moved to the tenth position.

When wishing to exit the maṇḍala, one must again follow the previous sequence of the five offerings and the five repentances to send [the deities] back; this constitutes the ninth, the practice of circumambulation (*caryā-pradakṣiṇa*). This is indeed the performance of the circumambulation.

Regarding the method of *fanbai* (Buddhist chanting): it is precisely when a ritual service is about to conclude that one again employs the practices previously cultivated to enter into mystical resonance with the ocean-like treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa*), thereby expressing the intent of "clinging" [to the Dharma].

Thus, while the underlying principles are identical, the purpose differs between the initial and subsequent stages. One then re-forms the mudrās of the three families, which are the three refuges (*triśaraṇa*).
Consequently, although there is a difference between the preceding and succeeding parts, there is no distinction in the liturgical text; this may be verified through the sequence.

The same. The unity of Exoteric and Esoteric Buddhism: the ten categories of clarifying the Dharma are all causes for the Esoteric; through the empowerment of the three mysteries, they equally accomplish the Exoteric contemplation.
Next, regarding the method of the ten intentions: first, to adorn and prepare the ritual arena (*maṇḍala*); second, to purify the three karmas; third, to perform offerings with the three karmas;
fourth, to invite the Triple Gem and the various devas; fifth, to offer praise and express sincerity; sixth, to prostrate; seventh, to recite mantras.
Eighth, the practice of the five repentances; ninth, walking the path and circumambulating; tenth, entering *samādhi*.

During the first period of entering the *maṇḍala*, one fully cultivates these ten dharmas. In each subsequent period, the invocation of the Buddha is omitted; the remaining nine practices are performed without difference.
Furthermore, one should employ the *Fahua Sanmei Zuboyi* (The Ritual for Assisting the Lotus Samādhi) to contemplate the phrases and verses, applying them to the ritual procedures.

At the conclusion of the ritual procedures, when one is engaged in formal cultivation, one should unify [the practice] through the contemplation of the principle of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-śūnyatā*) to achieve their mutual integration.

One should know that these ten [practices] each possess both the phenomenal and the noumenal; they all pertain to resonance and response, pervade the three karmas, completely purify the three obstructions, and fully realize the three virtues.
This constitutes the orthodox path of samādhi for our school. Having contemplated in this manner, one should apply oneself to further cultivation; thus, it is not the same as [other approaches].
To take the altar and mudrās as one’s sole destination, and to regard the mere preservation of syllables and sounds as the ultimate goal—this is how it is.

First, regarding the solemn preparation of the ritual site (*maṇḍala*), it is explained that one first prepares the site and decorates the images, and subsequently explains the binding of the boundary (*sīmābandha*). One should select an excellent location and dig a pit one cubit deep (using the Buddha-cubit).

[The ground shall be] three chi and six cun. Remove the old soil and take fresh earth from elsewhere to fill it and level it (in high plateaus or on the banks of great rivers, one should excavate to a depth of five chi or more;
such soil is considered new). Again, take pure earth and mix it with powdered incense. Measuring four *hasta* across, construct a square maṇḍala.

[According to the sūtra, the altar should be smeared with earth mixed with *gomaya* (cow dung). This must be the dung dropped by a white cow from the Snowy Mountains that eats only fatty, rich fodder; it is fragrant and pure and thus suitable for use. Since this is difficult to obtain in this region, use incense instead.]
On the ground, suspend a precious canopy. On all four sides, hang silk banners, streamers, colored pennants, white fans, and white whisks.

In the center, enshrine the image of the Principal Deity, the Mother of Ten Million Buddhas (facing west; this seating arrangement was originally devised by the Sage. According to the four types of *homa*, the *puṣṭi-homa* must indeed face west.

Since the present practice concerns supramundane *siddhi*, follow the ancient prescriptions, or adapt as appropriate to the circumstances). If the Principal Deity is unavailable, enshrine whatever [image] is available.
Buddha images, śarīra relics, and Mahāyāna sūtras or dhāraṇīs may also be used. The practitioner should set up a separate low seat and arrange these items facing the image.

Fearing that the ground may be damp or low-lying, one should spread mats and rugs all around. Furthermore, one should sprinkle the ritual area with scented water and inspect every part to ensure it strictly conforms to the prescribed regulations.
On the first day of the construction (which should be an observance day), one enters the maṇḍala using white sandalwood incense.
Construct eight maṇḍalas, resembling the full moon (these eight maṇḍalas are the objects of the samādhis of the eight great bodhisattvas;
they are the root-heart mahāvidyās of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas. Amoghavajra’s translation refers to them as "nine holy positions," which is merely a designation that includes the Buddha-mother).
Then, using fresh and pure offering vessels, arrange therein various foods and drinks, as well as fine incense, flowers, lamps, and *argha* perfumed water, according to one's means.

I offer this worship with a devoted heart and exhausted intent, making it pure and refined according to the Dharma. Why is this? Because my inner mind reveres the Triple Gem, which transcends the three realms;
now that I wish to invite and make offerings to them, how could I act with a frivolous mind? If I do not dedicate my own wealth and resources, [the offering will be incomplete].
If one makes offerings to the Mahāyāna, how then can one summon and inspire the worthy ones and sages, extinguish grave transgressions, and achieve the wondrous fruit?
Regarding the delimitation of the boundary (*sīmābandha*), the Sūtra says: "If one desires to seek a vow, one must first perform recitation and empower scented water."
Scatter [the flowers] throughout the eight directions, above, and below to form a boundary.
At the four sides of the maṇḍala, the practitioner should first mark the boundaries using either five-colored threads or railings to demarcate the place of practice.
When entering the maṇḍala, one should visualize that the Buddhas of the ten directions and the Honored One, the Buddha-Mother, are about to take their seats, and burn incense.

Scattering flowers, they waited with solemnity and joy. They then took pure water and recited a mantra over it one hundred and eight times, sprinkling it in the four directions, above, and below, thereby performing the rite of establishing the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*).
The *Ritual for Recitation Purifying the Three Karmas* states:

"In whatever place one dwells, bathe for purification, don fresh and clean robes, cultivate the four great vows amidst the four modes of deportment, and maintain an undistracted mind regarding all activities. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Samādhi* states: "First..."
Upon entering the maṇḍala, one should bathe with fragrant water and put on clean garments—either the great robe (saṃghāṭī) or various newly dyed robes.
If no new ones are available, one should take the finest among one's own clothes to serve as the attire for entering the maṇḍala.
Thereafter, if one leaves the *maṇḍala* and goes to an impure place, one should remove the pure robes and put on impure ones.
When the task is completed, one should bathe and put back on the original pure robes to enter the *maṇḍala* and perform the ritual. The *Mahākaruṇā-samādhi* states:
"Even if one does not go to a defiled place for an entire day, one must still bathe once; throughout the duration of the practice, one must remain focused and not allow for distraction."

Regarding speech and all social interactions, greetings, and inquiries, one must maintain this until the end of one's life. Following the sūtras, one should cultivate contemplation, never allowing for even a single moment of thought toward worldly affairs.
Even when attending to the necessities of defecation, urination, eating, or drinking, one must remain vigilant and guarded, ensuring that the practice is not lost or neglected.

Upon completing these tasks, one shall immediately enter the *dōjō*. One must not delay by making excuses for various matters. The essential points are: regarding the body, it concerns what is permitted and what is prohibited;
regarding the mouth, it concerns speaking and silence; regarding the mind, it concerns *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).

The Threefold Offering of Body, Speech, and Mind (*Zhiguan* states: "One performs the threefold offering by burning incense and directing the mind. When the practitioner first enters the *maṇḍala*, they proceed before the Dharma seat, spread out their sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), straighten their body, join their palms, and stand leaning slightly. They contemplate thus: 'For the sake of all sentient beings, I have resolved upon Bodhicitta;

I give rise to loving-kindness and exercise compassion, vowing to rescue and deliver them. With a sense of shame and deep sincerity, they visualize the Triple Gem filling the void of space, appearing as reflections within the *maṇḍala*. Holding an incense burner in hand, they burn various famous incenses and chant the Three [Refuges] with their mouth."*)
[Prostrate with] the five limbs touching the ground. [The leader says:
"With all reverence" (hereafter, all speak with one voice):

"With single-minded devotion, we prostrate at the feet of the Buddhas who eternally abide throughout the ten directions and the entire dharma-realm. [Follow the mind with the body and speech; prostrate with single-minded devotion without any thought of distraction. Understand that this body is like a shadow.]
[The subject] is unreal; the one who prostrates and the object of prostration are both unapprehendable by the mind. All sentient beings likewise enter this ocean of the Dharma-realm.

With single-minded devotion, prostrate with the crown of the head to the eternally abiding Dharma of the ten directions and the Dharma-realm (this and the following [sections on] the Sangha’s use of the mind are as above).

With single-minded devotion, prostrate to the eternally abiding Sangha of the ten directions and the entire Dharma-realm. (Having completed the prostrations to the Triple Gem, kneel facing one another while burning incense. Holding flowers in their hands, the leader says:)
All these assemblies, each kneeling in turn and reverently holding incense and flowers, made offerings according to the Dharma (hereafter, the assembly chanted in unison):
"May these clouds of incense and flowers fill the worlds of the ten directions; in every single Buddha-land, may they be adorned with immeasurable fragrances."

Fully endowed with the Bodhisattva path, one accomplishes the fragrance of the Tathāgata. (Visualize thus: "May these fragrant flowers of mine pervade the ten directions, forming a subtle and wondrous pavilion of light.

With celestial music and celestial precious incense, celestial delicacies and celestial precious garments, and the inconceivable dust-particles of the sublime Dharma—each single particle giving rise to all particles, each single particle giving rise to all dharmas—they revolve without obstruction, mutually adorning one another.

Reaching before the Triple Gem throughout the ten directions and the dharma-realm, may my own body everywhere perform offerings. Each and every offering pervades the entire dharma-realm; they are distinct yet unconfused, without hindrance or obstruction, performing the work of the Buddha until the end of the future."

May it universally permeate all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm; through this permeation, may they all give rise to the bodhicitta, together enter the state of non-arising, and realize Buddha-wisdom. Having visualized this, arise (perform the initial *śirṣa-bandha*).
Having made these offerings, all pay homage with reverence (one prostration).

They invite the Triple Gem and the celestial beings four times (having mentally performed the offerings, they kneel with one knee raised and burn incense). They should reflect that although the Triple Gem is free from obstructions and pure, they nevertheless protect and mindfully regard all classes of beings through their compassion of same-nature. If one can extend this invitation through the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, they will surely come even if not invited; they shall pull [beings] out [of suffering].

Regarding suffering and joy: the ritual for recitation states that the Buddha-mother Cundī, together with the eight great bodhisattvas and the assembly of holy beings, surrounded by their retinues, do not depart from their original lands but come to the place of practice and abide in the air to receive my offerings.

Therefore, now at each position, one should earnestly make three requests; there will surely be a response through divine descent. Below this, at each position, burn incense, kneel alternately, and make three requests. When the requests are finished, rise and prostrate.
With single-minded devotion, we offer this invocation: *Namo* to the World-Honored One, the Mother of Seven Koṭis of Buddhas, the Original Teacher, Cundī.

(This is the original body of Vairocana Tathāgata, from whom our Original Teacher Śākyamuni manifested his traces. The *Vajrabodhi Recitation Ritual* states: "Visualize within the Akaniṣṭha celestial palace, amidst an assembly of Vairocana Tathāgata surrounded by Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages, that one invites the Holy One, the Mother Cundī.

This is the same as Amoghavajra’s translated version. The *Mahāyoga Tantra King* refers to her as the Great Illuminator Vajra Tathāgata. Regarding "Seven Koṭis," the Mahāyāna *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clarifies...)

The *Sūtra of the King of Adorned Jewels* and the *Ritual for Accomplishment from the Vidyādhara-piṭaka* clarify seventy-seven koṭis [of deities]; they differ only according to the capacities of sentient beings. One should visualize: "The nature of my three karmas is like space; so too is the Buddha-Mother Cundī.

Arising from the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) for the sake of sentient beings, she comes together with the assembly to receive this offering. For the subsequent Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and noble Saṅgha, one should simply modify the visualization according to their respective ranks, as well as their names, forms, and places of origin.

With single-minded devotion, we take refuge in and entreat the World-Honored One, Seven Koṭis of Cundī of the Past (the dhāraṇī currently recited was already spoken by these seven koṭis of Buddhas of the past).

With single-minded devotion, we take refuge in and entreat the World-Honored One, Cundī, currently existing in the seven koṭis [of worlds]. (The Sūtra says: "The Buddhas currently existing are now proclaiming this dhāraṇī.")

The *Recitation Ritual* states: "The Buddha-Mother Cundī is surrounded by seventy million Buddhas. The *Sūtra of the Adorned Jewel King* states: "At that time, seventy-seven million Buddhas appeared simultaneously before him, and the World-Honored One then spoke this mantra."
I single-mindedly entreat these very ones, the seven koṭis of Buddhas of the present.
Homage to the seven koṭis of Bhagavatīs Cundā of the future. (The Sūtra says: "The Buddhas of the future shall all proclaim this mantra.")

This is the single-minded invocation of the ten World-Honored Buddhas of the ten directions, including the seven koṭis of future Buddhas, beginning with the Buddha of Good Virtue in the East. Homage to them!
With single-minded devotion, I make this invocation: *Namo to the Seven Koṭi Tathāgatas, the Praise of the Three Bodies, and the Cundī Dhāraṇī*.

(Recite the visualization as follows: "The nature of phenomena is like space, invisible; the eternally abiding Dharma-jewel is inconceivable. I now invoke you with my three karmas according to the Dharma; I pray that you will manifest and accept these offerings. The same applies below.)
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to all the *dhāraṇīs* subsumed within the five families, and to all the honored teachings of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Honored One, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Cundī. (The *Mahāyoga-tantra-rāja-sūtra* states: "Visualize the Honored One...")

The syllable transforms into Great Wisdom (*mahājñāna*). Great Wisdom transforms into the Bodhisattva Cundā. She is praised and described as the three bodies (*trikāya*) of seven *koṭi* Tathāgatas. Regarding her iconography, she has twenty-six arms and three faces, each face having three eyes.

The two scriptures, the *Vajrajñāna* and the *Amogha*, clarify that she has one face, three eyes, and eighteen arms. The *Sādhanavidhi of the Vidyottama-tantra* states: "If Cundā is taken as the central deity of the family, then place Cundā in the center.

Visualize the Bodhisattva Cundā with eighteen arms and three eyes on each face," and so forth. The Bodhisattvas and holy ones may be arranged according to one's preference. The syllable *Oṃ* is Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata; the syllable *La* is Mahācakra-vighnāntaka; the syllable *Lre* is Acala-vighnāntaka. [End.]

The syllable *A* is Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; the syllable *Li* is Amoghapāśa Bodhisattva; the syllable *Zun* is the Honored One, Cundā Bodhisattva; the syllable *Ni* is Vajrasattva; the syllable *Sha* is Ekajaṭī Bodhisatva; the syllable *He* is Vajranakhī Bodhisattva.
*Uṣṇīṣa* refers to the signless Dharmadhātu, which is Vairocana, appearing above the eight bodhisattvas. Now, these are the names of the eight bodhisattvas as they truly emerge.

However, by means of these nine subtle syllables, the Tathāgata establishes the nine holy ones—the Buddhas and Bodhisattva Vidyārājas—to represent the sovereign mastery of the compassion and wisdom of Cundā Bodhisattva, her manifold skillful means, her profound compassionate heart, and her great manifestation of majestic power.

[The practitioner] becomes wrathful, upholds and practices [the mantra], and dispels all obstacles; at once, they receive transformation and accomplish the path to Bodhi. This, in brief, clarifies the visualization of the *yoga* of the manifest tutelary deity (*iṣṭadevatā*).
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat: Namo to the Bodhisattva Mahācakra-vikrāmin; Namo to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Acala-vikrāmin.
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat: Namo to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara; Namo to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi.
With single-minded devotion, we take refuge in and entreat: Namah to the Bodhisattva Amoghapāśa;
the Bodhisattva Ekajaṭā; and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajranakhi.
With single-minded devotion, we pay homage to all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
With single-minded devotion, we pay homage to Mahākāśyapa and the entire assembly of great Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas,
and noble Saṃgha.
With single-minded devotion, I invoke the Bodhisattva Aparājita, the Bodhisattva Tārā, the Bodhisattva Hārītī, and the entire assembly of Great Wrathful Vidyārājas.
(At this point, one may burn incense and perform the invocation while standing; bhikṣus need not prostrate, whereas laypeople must do so.

Aparājita was originally the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha, who externally manifests as a Great Wrathful Vidyārāja within the Buddha Family. He occupies the position on the right, while his consort occupies the left. Both the translations by Śubhakarasiṃha and Vajrabodhi exist; the Sanskrit name is *Aparājita*.)

The Noble Tārā is a retinue member of Avalokiteśvara. Her form is that of a middle-aged woman; she holds a blue lotus with palms joined, wears a bright white robe, and smiles. She is a Vidyārājñī (Queen of Knowledge). Each of these two [deities] has its own separate sūtras and dhāraṇīs.

Hārītī is a yakṣiṇī, namely the Mother of Demons (Guizimu), who has five hundred retinue members. In the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, she is listed alongside the Four Kings and Guhyapati (Vajrapāṇi). The *Yogācāryabhūmi-rāja-sūtra* states:

"At that time, the Tathāgata Samantaprabhā-vajra entered the Vajra-samādhi of the 'Excellent Accomplishment of the Joyful Assembly of the Yakṣiṇī Hārītī. Having emerged from this meditative absorption, he then spoke the mantra of the Yakṣiṇī Hārītī. As for the ritual of this mantra, it is able to cause all yakṣas..."

The female ḍākinīs and others all appear before the practitioner to perform the rites of accomplishment. While they are originally wrathful vidyārājas, according to the two previous translations of the sūtra, they are now designated as bodhisattvas.
With single-minded devotion, we invoke the Great Brahmā, Lord of Devas; the Thirty-three Gods; the Four World-Protecting Kings;
the deities of the eight classes; the two Sons of the Pure Abodes; the two Dragon Kings, Nanda and Upananda; the auspicious palace gates; the hosts of Vidyādhara sages;
and all the numinous shrines of the great mountains and rivers within this realm, as well as the local spirits and deities belonging to the territory of this province. In this place...
[The place of residence. The guardian deity of the monastery. All the assembly of noble ones.
(Having completed the invitation, the presiding officiant states the purpose of the invocation:
"I pray that our Original Teacher, the Seven-Crore Tārā Buddha-Mother, the Tathāgatas of the Three Times Tārā, and those of the ten directions..."

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, without departing from the primordial limit, having been perfumed by impartial compassion, descended to the site of enlightenment to witness my practice of the Dharma.
This *Cundī Dhāraṇī*, spoken by the Mother of Seven Koṭis of Buddhas, is a secret essential of the Middle Way, manifested at the site of enlightenment.
May the Honored One, the Great Being Bhṛkuṭī Tārā, the Great Wheel Acala, and the bodhisattvas of this same maṇḍala,
by the power of their original vows, come to this place of practice, bestow the empowerment of divine mantras, and fulfill all wishes according to one's heart. Mahākāśyapa and all...
Great Śrāvakas, who equally exercise compassion, descend together at this very moment;
together with the Bodhisattva Aparājita Tārā, the Mother Hārītī, and all the Great Vidyārājas, we pray that you will preach the Dharma for us.
Bestowing the medicine of Dharma, dispelling all demonic obstacles, and manifesting auspiciousness,
may Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Great Kings, the eight classes of devas, nāgas, and others, as well as the sons of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens and the vidyādhara sages, follow my invitation and arrive.
Firmly maintain the site of practice (*maṇḍala*). Protect the boundaries of the nation. Ensure that what I cultivate does not deviate from my original vow.

(Perform a single prostration. The Fifth: Extolling with Sincerity. (Face the Dharma seat. Burn incense and scatter flowers. Contemplate in mind the subtle and wondrous merits of the Triple Gem. Furthermore, realize that the actions of body, speech, and mind pervade the entire Dharma-realm. Extol the Triple Gem as being without birth or extinction, and devoid of intrinsic nature. The Original Scripture.)
There is no extant text for this praise; I have now selected the *Dhāraṇī-kośa-gāthā* of Nāgārjuna’s *Cundā-bhagavatī-dhāraṇī* to serve as its eulogy:
With constant great compassion, you subdue all sentient beings; Having perfected an ocean of merit and virtue, I therefore pay homage to you.
The principle of True Suchness is pure and singular; Free from desire, you destroy all realms of existence.
Benefiting sentient beings while abiding in tranquility—therefore I praise and pay homage to you.
Firmly upholding pure precepts and entering the gateway of liberation, Abiding in the realm of supreme merit—therefore I praise and pay homage to Tārā, the accumulation of virtues.
With a tranquil mind, constantly maintain [this practice] against all great calamities.
There is no one capable of causing harm, whether in the heavens or among humans.
Receiving blessings equal to those of a Buddha, and having encountered this wish-fulfilling jewel, one will certainly attain great enlightenment.
Thus, praising the Buddha’s merits, one practices the Mahāyāna, dedicates these unsurpassed roots of goodness, and offers merit to the various devas of the higher realms.
May the eight classes of dragon deities, the local spirits of this land, and those who protect the True Dharma,

as well as kings and sovereigns, the myriad people of the realm, teachers, monks, parents, spiritual friends, and donors— extending broadly to all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm— rely upon these roots of goodness to cultivate with equanimity.
May the ten non-virtues, the five heinous crimes, and the three obstructions be extinguished, and may the two types of adornments, merit and wisdom, be perfected.

To adorn [oneself], to open the gate of *dhāraṇī*, and to accomplish the path of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). (These three eliminate the obstacles and perfect the two kinds of adornment. From this point on, one cultivates the repentance and makes the correct vows.

If there are those who consider this to be too brief, or who have specific vows, they should speak according to their own wisdom as is appropriate. However, the matters sought must not increase the cycle of birth and death, and the mind employed must necessarily benefit all beings. Having finished the recitation, pay homage.)
Sixth, the performance of prostrations:

The essence of the Three Jewels is unconditional compassion; they constantly desire to deliver all sentient beings, yet because there is no spiritual capacity [in us], they cannot manifest a response. Now that I have offered this invitation and praise, their hidden response is not in vain; therefore, they are now as if standing before my very eyes.
Accept my prostrations. Burn various renowned incenses. Prostrate with the five limbs touching the ground.

With single-minded devotion, pay homage to the Original Teacher, the World-Honored One Seven-Crore Mother of Buddhas, Cundī. (Visualize and say: "The nature of the one who prostrates and the object of prostration is empty and quiescent;

the resonance between cause and response is inconceivable. My place of practice is like a jewel of Indra, within which the Buddha-Mother Cundī appears as a reflection. My own body and shadow appear before Cundī; I bow my head to her feet in refuge and homage. [Then follow the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas below.]
One should modify [the recitation] according to the specific stage. For example, regarding "Seven Koṭi Buddhas," one says "within the manifestation of the Seven Koṭi Buddhas," and so forth.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate at the feet of the past Seven Koṭi Bhagavatīs Tārās.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the seven koṭis of present Bhagavatīs Cundās.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the seven koṭis of future Bhagavatīs Cundās.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the World-Honored One of Virtuous Excellence in the eastern world-realm of Freedom from Sorrow.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the World-Honored One of Sandalwood Virtue in the southern world-realm of Joy.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the World-Honored One of Infinite Radiance in the western realm named Sukhāvatī.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the World-Honored One of Marks and Virtues in the northern realm of Akṣobhya.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the World-Honored One, Virtue of Freedom from Sorrow, in the world of Moonlight in the southeastern direction.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the World-Honored One, Jewel Bestower, in the world of Multitude of Marks in the southwestern direction.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the World-Honored One Flower Virtue in the world of Multitudinous Sounds in the northwest.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the World-Honored One Practice of the Three Vehicles in the world of Tranquility in the northeast.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the World-Honored One of Virtuous Brilliance in the vast world-realm below.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the World-Honored One of Vast Multitude of Virtues in the world-realm of Many Moons above.
With single-minded devotion, prostrate in homage. This is the Praise of the Three Bodies of the Seven Koṭis of Tathāgatas, together with the Cundī Dhāraṇī.

(Perform three prostrations. Contemplate as follows: "The Dharma-nature of true emptiness is like space; the eternally abiding Dharma-jewel is inconceivable. My body and shadow now appear before this Dharma-jewel; with single-minded devotion, I take refuge and prostrate according to the Dharma. The same applies below.)
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to all *dhāraṇīs* subsumed within the five families, and to all the honored teachings of the ten directions and three periods of time.

With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Honored One, the Great Bodhisattva Cundī. (Perform three prostrations while visualizing: "In order to seek the extinction of obstacles, I prostrate by touching my feet to the ground. This is the confession.)
Because he is the lord of repentance,
I prostrate with single-minded devotion to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vidyārāja Mahācakra.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vidyārāja Acalanātha.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Amoghapāśa.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ikārajāta.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajranakṣatra.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to Mahākāśyapa and the entire assembly of great Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and noble Saṅgha.
Seventh, this Mantra Way is vast and perfectly integrated; its true reality is signless, free from all conceptual discrimination, and its nature is identical to space.
It is fully endowed with the three virtues, neither vertical nor horizontal, equally negating and upholding, and constitutes a mass of merit for all Buddhas.
Within this, the immovable suchness and the one hundred and sixty states of mind are perfectly transcended and unimpeded;

yet sentient beings do not realize or attain them for themselves, following along with ignorance and sinking together through the three realms of existence, like holding a burning ember that spins without ceasing.

When I examine the origins of this, I see that [the failure to realize it] is due to the fault of mere seeing and hearing. Therefore, the Tathāgata Cundā, whose compassion is boundless, has manifested traces from the fundamental source;
through the sudden transformation of the three mysteries, these traces descend from the source, and the nine syllables are simultaneously revealed.

These manifest as the color-form of the wisdom-ground that accords with reality, and as the vocal conditions of the teaching-gate. Flowing forth in accordance with the essence, they coalesce into Sanskrit characters, desiring to cause all beings—
Birth gives rise to the wisdom and vision of wondrous enlightenment and perfects the inherently existing body of gnosis.

These very sights and sounds are yet not sights and sounds; the forms and voices of the dharma-realm are identical in their ultimate reality. Now, the principle of the primary truth is fundamentally without sound or character.
The functions of sound and letters constitute a single gateway to principle. By relying on sound, one enters into wisdom; by means of letters, one exhausts the nature [of phenomena].

Apart from sound and letters, there is likewise no liberation. For practitioners today who set their minds upon practice and establish their conduct to shatter hindrances and manifest the principle, if they do not employ letters and rely on sound to enter samādhi, there will be no way to take the path home, nor to realize the fruit through its causes.
Therefore, this method of cultivation establishes two gates: namely, the retention of syllables arranged upon sound, and the retention of entering into samādhi.
Nāgārjuna names these the "retention with signs" (*sanimitta-dhāraṇī*) and the "signless retention" (*animitta-dhāraṇī*).

The signless retention will be explained in the tenth chapter. Regarding the retention with signs: examine these sounds and syllables; they are both material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) and collectively constitute the essence of the teaching (*deśanā-śarīra*). [End of fragment]
The *Myōon* (Singing Cloud) states: "The nature of form (*rūpa*) is itself wisdom; it is called the Wisdom Body (*jñānakāya*). Tiantai refers to this as the body of the Dharma-gate of mindfulness.
The *Niansong yi* (Ritual for Recitation) states: "From the crown of the head to the feet, one arrays the nine Brahma-syllables upon the practitioner’s body.
Thus, by arraying the syllable *Oṃ* at the crown, one accomplishes the All-Encompassing Wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*). By arraying the syllable *Ja*..."
The two pupils of the eyes constitute the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional. By arranging the character *li* (戾) on the left and right eyes, one achieves compassion.
By arranging the character *zhu* (主) at the neck and throat, one achieves unimpeded eloquence.
By arranging the character *li* (戾) on the left and right shoulders, one achieves the Four Great Vows. By arranging the character *zhun* (准) at the heart, one achieves... [the four immeasurables].
This is the Tathāgatagarbha. By placing the syllable *Ṭi* at the navel, the three samādhis are accomplished.

By placing the syllable *Svāhā* on both thighs, the pāramitā of earth is accomplished (the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states that the ten stages are the feet; the Tiantai commentary explains that the ten perfections are the feet of the ten stages).
By placing the syllable *Ha* on both feet, meditative concentration and wisdom are perfected. In this manner, all these dharmas aggregate and join together to form the body.
Since the nature of form is already wisdom, the nature of wisdom is also form. When this body of wisdom is fully manifested, obstructions are thereby shattered and virtues are revealed through it.
Above, it merges with the essence of the Dharma; below, it responds to all sentient beings, manifesting the form of the retributive wisdom-body.
It is here that completion is achieved. Furthermore, one should know that by entering the nine Brahma-gate syllables, one enters the stages of the nine sages and worthies.

Cause and effect are unified, and the physical body and the Dharma-nature are merged in profound stillness. Thus, one achieves a body empowered by the Tathāgata’s seal and the eight great Bodhisattvas.
Although their original and manifested forms differ, they are non-conceptually one; it is for this reason that this is called the "Excellence Dharma Gate. Since—
Once the arrangement is complete, one then recites aloud. As for the method of recitation: first, realize that the nature of sound is empty and the color of the characters is signless.
The sound is neither slow nor hurried; the characters have no sequence of before or after. The nature of the mind is devoid of inherent existence, and the mind does not diverge from its object.
The modulated *brahman* sounds and the nine *brahman* syllables are distinct and clear. The body of the mantra thus arrayed is identical to the nine holy marks.
With clear and unclouded awareness, maintain this mindfulness in this way. Advancing without ceasing, discern each detail until there is no interval between light and darkness;
naturally, you will then behold the marks and signs of the Honored One, radiant with light, surrounded by his retinue, sitting in face-to-face presence with you.

This is the method for the dhāraṇī of the sound of the arrayed syllables (Buzi yuansheng chi fa). [With body upright and majestic deportment, burning incense and scattering flowers, they chant these vows with one voice:
"I, [Name], now wish to perform recitation. I pray that the Honored Ones, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, will grant their empowerment and protective mindfulness.

May I swiftly attain my desires, and may the siddhi sought be fully perfected. (After chanting this three times, perform one prostration. The verse for the arraying of syllables says: First, contemplate the perfectly luminous, formless body. With *Oṃ*...)

Spread across the crown, it forms the seed of omniscience; folded and spread over the pupils, it clarifies the two truths. Bent and spread over the two eyes, it gazes with compassion; spread over the neck and throat, it masters unimpeded discernment. Bent and spread over the two shoulders, the great vows reside there; aligned and spread, it is the Tathāgata’s secret treasury of the mind.

Place the three *samādhis* at the navel and waist with the syllable *Ti*. Place *Sva-bha* on the thighs and knees. Place *Ha* on both feet to perfect concentration and wisdom. Having thus visualized the arrangement of these syllables, one immediately accomplishes the supreme Dharma-gate of Cundī.
(The first section concerns the white [mantra] and the origin of the recitation.)

At that time, out of compassion for future sentient beings of meager merit and evil karma, the World-Honored One entered the Cundī Samādhi and spoke the dhāraṇī taught by seven hundred million past Buddhas.
(The assembly together bound the ritual mudrās with their hands and recited the mantra with their mouths:)

Mentally visualize the spreading of the Brahma-net. As for the method of its mudrā: interlace the little fingers and ring fingers of both hands and insert them into the palms. Straighten and erect the two middle fingers so that they support one another. Place the two index fingers against the upper joints of the two middle fingers.
Place the two thumbs against the sides of the two index fingers. This completes it.
Namo saptānām (1) samyaksaṃbuddhakoṭīnām (2) tadyathā (3) oṃ cale (4) cule (5) cuḍe (6) svāhā (7).

it is because those who recite and maintain [the teachings] by relying on the arrangement of characters and the conditions of sound, according to the Dharma, as in the "Peaceful Practices" (Anrakugyō) chapter of the Lotus Sūtra, do not enter samādhi but practice while walking or standing and recite and maintain [the text].
One will also behold the sublime and wondrous form of Samantabhadra. As for the practitioner who enters samādhi and maintains it:

they should focus their mind on the practice, enter samādhi, sit with the body upright and eyes closed, and clarify the mind while quieting the thoughts. Then, a brilliant, luminous clarity will manifest vividly within the chest.
Like the full moon, within its perfect luminosity, one contemplates the nine seed-syllables beginning with Oṃ;
by entering the gateway of the Svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī, one will surely behold the fundamentally pure mind, which accords with the Prajñāpāramitā.
When concentration and wisdom manifest before one, one enters and realizes the ten stages (*bhūmi*). The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* states:
"While the practitioner is engaged in walking, sitting, or recitation, body and mind become tranquil, like empty space.

Entering into various states of profound meditative absorption, within right wisdom they behold Samantabhadra Bodhisattva face-to-face, riding a six-tusked white elephant and surrounded by immeasurable bodhisattvas. By means of this—
The body that is pleasing for all sentient beings to behold appears before them.
Because these people see Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, they immediately attain samādhi and dhāraṇī. Samādhi is concentration (samatha); dhāraṇī is wisdom (prajñā).
This is the manifestation of the purification of the two roots of concentration and wisdom. One must further examine in detail the three types of siddhi in the Susiddhikara Sūtra.
